slides.heading: Week 8: Ethics, Privacy and Copyright
slides.narration: [warmly] Welcome back to Ground School. I'm Captain Naomi, and this is Week 8: ethics, privacy and copyright. It's a serious one, so we'll take it steadily, the same way you'd fly through weather you respect.

slides.heading: Mission Brief
slides.narration: Here's the mission brief: protect information, credit work and respect consent. Three areas. Privacy, which means protecting your own information and other people's. Creative work, where you'll learn to keep permission, attribution and AI disclosure as three separate questions. And harmful media, where you'll learn to recognise the boundary and know exactly how to get help.

slides.heading: Before this lesson
slides.narration: Before we start, one thing. You do not need to share personal experiences in this lesson. In class discussion, use the fictional examples only. If a topic feels close to home, pause and speak privately with a trusted adult. And it's your choice: you never need to show anyone upsetting material to join the activity.

slides.heading: Three fictional scenarios
slides.narration: We'll work with three fictional scenarios. First, private messages: a student uploads a friend's chat to analyse what it means. Second, a generated song: a student imitates a named artist and claims the result is entirely their own. Third, a fake classmate image: a student makes a humiliating fake image, as a joke. Keep all three in mind. We'll come back to each one.

slides.heading: Start with four questions
slides.narration: Every one of these starts with four questions. The big one: who is affected by this choice? Then information: whose data, message or image is involved? Permission: what did they agree to, and for which use? And consequences: who might be misled, exposed or harmed? Run that checklist before you upload, generate or share anything.

slides.heading: Privacy: information leaves a boundary
slides.narration: Privacy first. When you use a cloud tool, it processes what you send. A cloud chatbot handles your submitted content through its own service, so that content has left your device. Settings differ: storage, memory and whether your chats can be used for future training all depend on the service and its controls. So here's your rule. Do not submit sensitive information, or other people's private information.

slides.heading: Never-share information
slides.narration: Some information stays off the list entirely. Use fictional examples and placeholders instead. Accounts: passwords, authentication codes and identity documents. Identifying details: your home address, phone number, school identifiers and personal images. And other people: their private messages, records or photos that they haven't agreed to share.

slides.heading: Scenario 1: a safer alternative
slides.narration: So, back to scenario one. A safer prompt looks like this: "A fictional friend replies briefly to a message. Give several possible explanations without claiming to know their thoughts." You use an invented situation. And if a real misunderstanding matters to you, talk respectfully to the person, rather than uploading their private chat.

slides.heading: Anonymising is more than removing a name
slides.narration: You might think, fine, I'll just delete the names. But anonymising is more than removing a name, because details can still identify someone. Possible clues include a location, a date, a unique event or someone's role. For this course, the better option is a completely fictional scenario. And if you're unsure, do not upload it. Ask a trusted adult how to proceed.

slides.heading: Three settings to review
slides.narration: There are three settings worth reviewing in any AI service. Model improvement: can your conversations be used for future model training? Memory: what personalisation information is retained or referenced? And history and deletion: how do you manage your chats and any connected information?

slides.heading: Memory and chat deletion differ
slides.narration: Here's a detail that catches people out. Memory and chat deletion are different controls, so check the relevant ones. Turning memory off does not necessarily delete your existing chats. And deleting a chat may not remove a memory that was saved separately. Review these together, using the service's current settings and help pages.

slides.heading: Pilot's Tip: use the settings as evidence
slides.narration: Pilot's Tip: use the settings as evidence. A chatbot's self-report is not a full data audit. You may ask it, "What do you remember about me?" Then verify, by reviewing the memory and data controls that are actually available. Think of it like checking the instruments, not just asking the plane how it feels. For the class log, record only the categories you checked, not private contents or screenshots.

slides.heading: AI companions are products
slides.narration: Now, AI companions. They are products, and friendly responses are not human care. A system can produce personal-sounding or reassuring language. That does not establish human understanding, feelings or a dependable relationship. So for difficult experiences, talk with a trusted person or a qualified support service.

slides.heading: Copyright basics
slides.narration: On to copyright. Creative expression has legal protections. Examples include writing, images, music, recordings and code. The key distinction: an idea and its particular expression are not the same thing. So before you reuse anything, check for permission, the licence conditions, or an exception that actually applies.

slides.heading: Australia: fair dealing has conditions
slides.narration: In Australia, we have fair dealing, and it has conditions. Do not assume there's a blanket fair use permission. The exceptions cover specific purposes, including research or study, criticism or review, and parody or satire. Even then, the purpose and the conditions must fit your actual use. The practical approach: use original material, or a suitable licence, whenever you can.

slides.heading: Permission, credit and disclosure
slides.narration: Three separate questions for any creative work. Permission: am I allowed to use this material in this way? Attribution: who created the source material, and what credit is required? And AI disclosure: what did the AI contribute, and what did I do? Answering one doesn't answer the others.

slides.heading: Style is not a blanket clearance
slides.narration: Style is not a blanket clearance, so check the actual material and the claims you make. A broad influence is different from copying recognisable protected expression. There are other risks too: false endorsement, misleading attribution, and the rules of the tool or your school still matter. For this assignment, develop your own creative choices, and describe any AI help honestly.

slides.heading: Scenario 2: a safer alternative
slides.narration: Back to scenario two, the generated song. The safer path: describe the musical qualities you want, develop your own lyrics and composition, credit any reused material, and disclose generated contributions accurately. What not to do: don't claim a named artist made or endorsed the work, and don't present generated material as entirely unaided human work.

slides.heading: AI output does not settle ownership
slides.narration: AI output does not settle who owns something, so keep the evidence of your work. Retain your drafts, sources, licences and decisions. Follow your school, competition and platform requirements. And do not assume that a prompt, a credit line or a few edits guarantee legal ownership.

slides.heading: What is a deepfake?
slides.narration: Now the harder part of today. What is a deepfake? It's a manipulated depiction of someone. It can take the form of images, video or audio. The deception is that a person appears to say or do something they did not. And the boundary is clear: do not create humiliating, sexual or otherwise abusive depictions of real people.

slides.heading: Consent is specific
slides.narration: Consent is specific. A photo being available is not permission to misuse it. A shared photo does not give blanket permission for new edits or wider sharing. A private message does not become yours to redistribute. And pressure, or calling it a joke, does not remove responsibility for the harm.

slides.heading: Australian law: harmful sexual deepfakes
slides.narration: Here's where Australian law comes in. Non-consensual sharing of sexual deepfakes can be criminal. Federal offences cover using a carriage service, which means things like the internet or a phone network, to transmit sexual material without consent, and that includes qualifying deepfakes. Creating them and other conduct can bring additional offences, and state or territory laws can apply too. The course boundary is simple: do not create, request or share sexual deepfakes.

slides.heading: Abusive material involving children
slides.narration: This next point matters. Generated does not mean exempt from the law. AI-generated sexual abuse material involving children can be illegal. If you encounter it, do not save it, screenshot it or forward it. Get help instead: tell a trusted adult, and follow eSafety or police guidance.

slides.heading: Non-sexual fakes can still cause harm
slides.narration: Not explicit doesn't mean harmless. Non-sexual fakes can still cause real harm: humiliation, bullying and damage to someone's reputation. Whether there's school action or legal consequences depends on the conduct and the circumstances. But your decision doesn't need to wait for that. Do not make or circulate humiliating fake images of classmates.

slides.heading: Scenario 3: a safer alternative
slides.narration: So, scenario three. The safer alternative is to not create or circulate the humiliating image in the first place. If one already exists, stop sharing it, and ask a trusted adult to help address the harm. And if you're working on a creative project, use original fictional characters and respectful material. No real classmate's likeness is needed.

slides.heading: If you or a friend is targeted
slides.narration: If you or a friend is targeted, there are three moves. Do not spread it: don't forward the image, and don't request a copy. Tell someone: ask a trusted adult, a teacher or the school counsellor for help. And report and get support, using eSafety guidance and appropriate support services.

slides.heading: Keep useful information safely
slides.narration: Keep useful information safely, but do not collect illegal images as evidence. With adult support, note the relevant links, account handles, dates and any report references. Here's an important boundary: do not save or share sexual images of anyone under eighteen. Follow the reporting instructions from eSafety or the police.

slides.heading: If someone threatens you
slides.narration: If someone threatens you, do not pay, and do not send more content. Stop contact, and don't negotiate with the person making threats. Ask for support: a trusted adult can help with reporting and with your account security. And hear this clearly. [short pause] Being targeted is not your fault, even if you shared something earlier.

slides.heading: Support in Australia
slides.narration: Here's where to find support in Australia. To report image-based abuse, go to esafety dot gov dot au. For counselling and support, there's Kids Helpline, on one eight hundred, fifty five, one eight hundred. That's free phone counselling, twenty four hours a day, seven days a week. And if you're in immediate danger in Australia, call Triple Zero, zero zero zero.

slides.heading: Support a friend without spreading the harm
slides.narration: If a friend comes to you, you can support them without spreading the harm. Listen, and help them find a trusted adult. You might say, "I'm glad you told me. You deserve help." Do not ask to see the image or to receive a copy. And keep boundaries: don't promise secrecy if someone is unsafe. Help them reach support.

slides.heading: Reporting is a step towards help
slides.narration: Reporting is a step towards help, and you don't have to wait until you're certain. If one adult doesn't help, tell another trusted adult. What you deserve is support, and a response focused on safety. What we can't promise is instant removal, or a particular school or legal outcome.

slides.heading: When should a human be accountable?
slides.narration: Let's zoom out. When should a human be accountable for a decision? Consider the consequence of a wrong one. The stakes are higher in health, education, money, justice or safety. There, you want safeguards: qualified review, a way to challenge the result, and clear responsibility. For your own project, decide which outputs need checking before anyone acts on them.

slides.heading: Try It Now
slides.narration: Try It Now. Rewrite the three scenarios from today. For each one, ask: what went wrong, and who was affected? Then, what should the student do instead? Use fiction only. Don't include real messages, names, images or allegations. Pause the video here and work through all three. [pause]

slides.heading: Common Turbulence: "It was a private chat"
slides.narration: Common Turbulence: "It was a private chat." A small audience does not remove the harm. Copies and screenshots can spread further than anyone planned. A private setting doesn't supply permission either. So your action stays the same: do not create, request or circulate abusive material.

slides.heading: Memory Hook
slides.narration: Here's your Memory Hook. My data. Their data. Their work. Their face. The instruction is to respect all four. And the habit is to pause before uploading, generating or sharing.

slides.heading: Pre-Landing Check 1
slides.narration: Pre-Landing Check one. Does calling a sexual deepfake a joke make it safe or lawful? Your turn. Explain the boundary, without assuming every case has identical legal facts. Pause the video and work out your answer. [pause]

slides.heading: Check 1: answer
slides.narration: No. A joke is not permission. The boundary: do not create, request or share sexual deepfakes. The law: criminal offences can apply, depending on the conduct and the circumstances. And the response: get adult support, and use authoritative reporting guidance.

slides.heading: Pre-Landing Check 2
slides.narration: Pre-Landing Check two. Where can you report image-based abuse in Australia? Your turn: name the service. Pause the video and say it out loud. [pause]

slides.heading: Check 2: answer
slides.narration: It's eSafety, at esafety dot gov dot au. For support, ask a trusted adult to help. On evidence, do not forward abusive images to prove what happened. And if you're in immediate danger, call Triple Zero, zero zero zero, in Australia.

slides.heading: Pre-Landing Check 3
slides.narration: Pre-Landing Check three. What makes a useful AI disclosure? Think back to Week 6: what does your reader need to know? Pause the video and jot down your answer. [pause]

slides.heading: Check 3: answer
slides.narration: A useful disclosure names specific contributions. The AI contribution: say what the tool suggested, edited or generated. Your contribution: say what you selected, changed and created. And remember it's a separate requirement. Disclosure does not replace permission to reuse material.

slides.heading: Home Lab: Ethics Casebook
slides.narration: Your Home Lab this week is an Ethics Casebook, in four parts. One, three cases: for each, the problem, the people affected and a safer alternative. Two, one new case: invent a non-graphic privacy, fairness or copyright scenario. Three, a settings check: review training use, memory and history, with adult support. Four, a design update: add relevant safeguards to your Week 7 pitch. Allow forty five to sixty minutes, and keep private contents and account screenshots out of your Project Log.

slides.heading: A privacy-check log without private data
slides.narration: Here's how to log your privacy check without any private data. Three rows. Model improvement: available setting reviewed. Memory: available controls reviewed. History and deletion: current help guidance reviewed. For each one, your follow-up is keep, change, or ask an adult. That's all the log needs.

slides.heading: Project Log: Entry 8
slides.narration: Project Log, Entry 8. Record your decisions without exposing people. For the casebook, that's your three rewrites and one fictional case. For settings, only the categories you reviewed and the actions you chose. And for safeguards, one update, and why it addresses a risk.

slides.heading: No-account option
slides.narration: If you don't have an account, there's a no-account option. Plan the privacy check on paper. Use the checklist to write what you would look for in a suitable service. Discuss which controls would need adult help. And do not claim that settings were changed or deleted when you only made a plan.

slides.heading: Parent & Guardian Brief
slides.narration: This one is for your parent or guardian. Make this a calm, private conversation. Listen: thank the learner for raising a concern, and avoid blame. Help: use eSafety guidance, school support and counselling when needed. And review the relevant parental controls and account privacy settings together.

slides.heading: Ready for Week 9
slides.narration: [warmly] That's Week 8 landed. This week you examined privacy, consent, attribution and harmful media. Next week is the Capstone Sprint, where you'll scope and build a project with evidence and safeguards. Until then, keep the habit: respect my data, their data, their work and their face. See you on the flight deck.
